Heavy rains and high winds downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia
Skies cleared along the US eastern seaboard on Friday, and power was being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers whose Thanksgiving plans were disrupted by heavy rains and high winds that swept over the region a day earlier.
The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. At its peak, nearly a million customers were without power .
The storms prompted the first-ever postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City, as well as the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights. In New Jersey widespread flooding reached levels not seen since 2012, after Hurricane Sandy.
By Friday morning, conditions had significantly improved, though hundreds of thousands remained without power and air travel was still affected by significant delays.
On Friday afternoon Poweroutage.us reported 400,577 customers were still without power, including 98,597 in Pennsylvania, 63,658 in Missouri and 60,297 in New Jersey.
Flightaware said delays within, into, or out of the US on Friday stood at 2,489, and cancellations at 144. On Thursday, more than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations had been delayed and more than 400 had been cancelled.
“The bulk of the storm impacts are behind us, but tidal flooding will continue today,” the National Weather Service said early Friday.
Parts of the midwest and the south were dealing with unusual snowfalls for the time of year, with St Louis, Missouri, getting 7.3in, and snow reported in Alabama and Tennessee. An ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3am, according to the city.
“The south and south-east US will start with very cold morning temperatures today and Saturday as lows drop into the upper 20s and the middle 30s,” the National Weather Service said. “Freeze headlines are in effect for portions of the deep south. High temperatures Saturday will begin to moderate into the 60s.”
In New York City, authorities were rushing to clean up the damage the storm left in its wake. Several people had to be rescued from their cars amid flooding, said Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
Strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, but no injuries were reported.
New York City police said they had recovered a body of man along the Staten Island shoreline. It was not yet clear if the death was storm-related.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through to New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey , scrambled to pump out saltwater on Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community’s history.
Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding had become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.
“Our family’s been here for 36 years,” McKenna said. “But honestly, we’re thinking is this the right place for us to be? We’re now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this?”
Donald Trump signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues.
The US president had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach. “Since October it has been raining continuously,” the president said. “It’s the craziest thing. It stopped now.”
Meanwhile, authorities on the west coast were assessing the damage from high-tide-driven waves and strong winds.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt county in the far north to Ventura county near Los Angeles.
Workers in Pacifica, California, rushed to evaluate the damage after part of the Pacifica pier collapsed into the ocean on Wednesday amid powerful waves.
The high tides continued to affect train service on Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.

Hamas chief's last surviving son escapes Israeli strike in Gaza
Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya’s last surviving son Izzeldeen survived an Israeli assassination attempt on Friday, senior Hamas official Basem Naim said. Four of Izzeldeen’s brothers were killed by Israeli forces, including his twin Hamam, who died in a 2025 airstrike in Qatar.

Four of Khalil al-Hayya’s other sons were previously killed by Israeli forces, according to the Palestinian group.
A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.
The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the strip killed four Palestinians, despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed over a year ago.
Izzeldeen al-Hayya, 29, and his family survived the Israeli strike at dawn, said Hamas official Basem Naim. Hamas sources told the Reuters news agency that several relatives were wounded, including the daughter-in-law of the Hamas chief.
The family of another of Khalil al-Hayya’s deceased sons, Azzam, also survived.
Naim described Izzeldeen as the Hamas leader’s last surviving son. Four of his brothers were killed by Israeli forces: Hamza in 2008, Osama in 2014, Humam in September last year and Azzam in May this year.
Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Humam, who was killed in an Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year. Khalil al-Hayya narrowly escaped that attack during negotiations. He was named leader of Hamas in July.
Hamas condemned Friday’s attack, describing it as an attempt to “assassinate” al-Hayya’s son and target his family.
The group linked the attack to threats made against its leader by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and accused Israel of seeking to undermine the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Hamas said the “cowardly act” exposes the “complete detachment from human and moral values” of Israeli leaders.
Deadly Israeli attacks continued elsewhere in Gaza on Friday.
A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in a drone att on a vehicle in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.
Wafa named the victim as Khaled Assaf and quoted witnesses as saying a vehicle was struck in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp.
In the southern city of Rafah, Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of three Palestinians and rescued two wounded people following an attack near Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, Wafa reported.
Israeli army gunfire injured a Palestinian child in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
Medical sources and witnesses told Wafa that Israeli forces repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced people in the area from their positions near the eastern “Yellow Line”.
Friday’s attacks followed a series of Israeli raids on Thursday that killed 10 Palestinians, including a senior education official.
Also on Friday, Hamas described as “ridiculous” the Israeli army’s claim that it used one of the buildings at Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza City as an interrogation centre.
The Israeli military and Shin Bet made the allegations on Thursday, claiming Hamas was conducting military activities within the hospital complex.
The Israeli claim “comes as part of the ongoing incitement against hospitals in the Gaza Strip”, Hamas said in a statement.
Hospitals are “public places open to all civil and UN institutions operating in the enclave”, it noted, adding that Israel had never provided evidence to substantiate any of its claims.
The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which oversees the hospital, said it had no knowledge of any secret interrogation centre on the premises.
According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the October 2025 “ceasefire” since it took effect have killed at least 1,705 Palestinians and wounded 6,163. Israel has killed at least 74,772 Palestinians in Gaza since the genocidal war began in October 2023.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition.
OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.
The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.
OpenAI is developing artificial intelligence-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf,” the company said in its Friday court filing.
OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware products.
“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.
Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.
In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former employees, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
The litigation sets up a battle over who will control future AI devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of its own.
In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticised Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs.
OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.
OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

An official inspects the partially submerged tanker - the rescue operation is expected to be challenging
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.
In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.
Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute.
The Marseille prosecutor’s office said it would open an investigation into the trouble, specifically accusations that French fans committed “aggravated intentional violence” against Levski supporters, and that it would also pursue allegations of “incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans”.
A statement on behalf of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, on Friday said he condemned the violence “in the strongest possible terms” and that it had “no place in sport or in public places”. He also insisted “these acts would not go unpunished”.
The Bulgarian president, Iliana Iotova, described the violence as “unacceptable” and “shocking” and said: “The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world. Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”
The country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said he had spoken to Macron about the incident which had resulted in 11 Bulgarian fans being hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilised Europe,” Radev said. “I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Another Europa League fixture on Thursday, between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer Sheva, was suspended for 30 minutes owing to fighting. Uefa’s account of the disruption that occurred at a neutral venue in Batumi, Georgia, said the game had been suspended to allow local police to subdue fighting between Besiktas supporters. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said some fans had been denied entry.
Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as “unacceptable” actions undertaken by Georgian police targeting Besiktas supporters who unfurled a pro-Palestine banner during the match.
A Uefa statement, however, said: “Uefa understands that the escalation between the local police and Besiktas’ supporters – which caused the temporary suspension of the match – started following an intervention of the local police in the sector of the Besiktas supporters to neutralise clashes that had erupted amongst Besiktas’ own supporters.”
Uefa condemned the violence at both matches and said it had appointed inspectors to conduct disciplinary investigations. “Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety,” a statement said. “The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values.” Any investigation would “examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances”, the statement said.
Last season Marseille were hit with a partial stadium closure after fans launched fireworks and pointed lasers into the field during a Champions League fixture against Atalanta.

Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.
Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.
On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.
He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.
Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.
He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.
Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies . People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases : children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.
Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.
The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.
President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.
Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

Spanish women’s refusal to surrender hard-won rights helped Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez stave off defeat in a snap election three years ago. As he gambles with another early vote on Sunday, his hopes of defying the odds rest on women again rallying to block the far right from governing Spain for the first time since Franco’s dictatorship.
Kicking off his latest mission impossible at a rally in Seville, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sported a red T-shirt with the slogan “ La fuerza de las Mujeres” (the strength of women) as he urged progressive voters to engineer an “epic comeback” at the polls.
After eight gruelling years in office, Spain ’s great political survivor knows he will need every bit of strength Spanish women can give him.
Voter surveys are predicting a decisive swing to the right in Sunday’s general election, potentially bringing a far-right party into government for the first time since Franco ’s death in 1975.
Watch more Sanchez's big gamble: Will Spain swing from Socialists to hard right?
It’s a familiar predicament for Sanchez, who has defied the odds in past elections – in large part thanks to the support of female voters determined not to surrender hard-won rights.
His Socialist Workers’ Party of Spain (PSOE) has framed the vote as a choice between “progress” and “regression”, warning that victory for a right-wing block that includes the hardline Vox party would rewind the clock to a time when Spanish women had far fewer rights.
The pitch has worked before, most recently in the last snap election Sanchez called in 2023. His chances of pulling off an even greater upset on November 29 rest largely on women's willingness to cast aside their grievances and bail him out once more.
Sanchez called the snap election on October 5 after right-wing parties voted down emergency measures his government had put together to tackle a housing crisis roiling the country.
The prime minister was hoping anger at the right for torpedoing the emergency measures would help his Socialists close the gap with the conservative Peoples’ Party (PP), which polls say is likely to secure a majority of seats in parliament in partnership with the anti-immigrant, anti-feminist Vox.
While surveys suggest the PSOE has indeed narrowed the gap, the combined left-wing bloc is still lagging far behind the joint tally of the conservatives and the far right , leaving Sanchez and his allies with a mountain to climb.

Demography is one reason the Socialists are actively courting the female vote, said Carmen Aguilera-Carnerero, a professor at the University of Granada whose research focuses on extremist rhetoric and the far right.
“There are roughly 1.2 million more women voters than there are men. That makes it a highly coveted constituency in an election that could end up being closer than expected,” she explained.
Aguilera-Carnerero said the Socialists were aiming to tap a large pool of potential voters among middle-aged women traditionally suspicious of extremist parties. She pointed to Sanchez’s widely commented appearance on the cover of a gossip magazine as part of efforts to appeal to that audience.
Sanchez has played up the legislation introduced under leftwing governments in recent decades aimed at bolstering women’s rights, such as access to abortion or better protection against gender-based violence. He has warned that a right-wing government that includes Vox would roll back decades of progress.

“Women who are in their 30s or 40s today, and have lived through different governments, are well aware of how their situation has changed and what has been achieved under left-wing governments in terms of the rights of women and minorities,” said Aguilera-Carnerero. “For many who haven’t lived through these transformations, however, the picture is perhaps less clear.”
Aguilera-Carnerero noted that “many first-time voters are unfamiliar with the Indignados Movement of 2011 – let alone the Franco era”. Young people, she added, “are looking for access to education, a job, a house, and many of them are probably not thinking so much about social rights and liberties”.
She warned that “playing the anti- fascist card” could alienate some voters and drive abstention in a country wearied by six general elections in 11 years – and also jar with the immediate concerns of many youths.
The government's failure in recent years to address the housing crisis and halt home evictions is one reason many progressive voters feel let down, said the Asambleas Feministas Abiertas de Cantabria, a feminist group based in northern Spain.
“There is fatigue, more than in 2023. People are exhausted by rent and precarity, and many feel the ‘progressive’ government didn’t deliver,” the group said in written exchanges with FRANCE 24.
“But it is fatigue with the parties, not resignation,” they added, highlighting the scale of the housing protests that have swept the country and the huge rallies against gender-based violence that took place in cities across the country this week.

“Feminist and housing movements are very active (...). The question is whether that energy turns into votes,” they added. “That depends on the left giving people a reason (to back them), not just a fear.”
While Vox's atavistic brand of macho chauvinism has long alienated female voters, surveys suggest fear of the far right has eroded in recent years, including among women.
According to polling institute 40dB, the proportion of female Vox supporters now stands at one for every 1.29 men, down from one for every 1.7 men only a year ago, narrowing the gender gap that once defined the party.
Aguilera-Carnero said Vox had recently played down some of its more divisive policies , such as repealing abortion rights or replacing the equality ministry introduced by the left with a family ministry tasked with promoting higher birth rates and traditional family values.
“That doesn’t mean their ideas have changed on these issues, but the focus has shifted,” she cautioned, noting that the party increasingly talks about the need to “protect” Spanish women.
“They claim that Spanish women need protection from outsiders, from immigrants who come from cultures that don’t respect women, and that if you stop immigration women will feel free and safe,” she explained, noting that this “femonationalist” stance was in line with other far-right movements in Europe.

Scapegoating immigrants is one example of what Aguilera-Carnero described as the “simple solutions to complex problems” that Vox claims to offer. Such “solutions” are channelled through the party’s unmatched use of social media to reach a young and disgruntled audience, the youngest of whom have only ever known left-wing governments.
While Vox has recently made inroads among female voters, angry young men remain its largest constituency, egged on by the party’s rants against “woke” ideas, feminism and what it describes as “gender ideology”.
The rise of masculinism among young Spaniards highlights a broader educational problem that the left has so far failed to address, said the feminist Asambleas in northern Cantabria.
“We see it in schools: the manosphere, influencers, the idea that feminism ‘has gone too far’. The far right offers precarious young men someone to blame, women and migrants, instead of the real causes,” they said. “The answer needs to be education from early childhood, not punishment: sex and emotional education, coeducation, other models of masculinity.”

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes last bid to beat right-wing parties before Spanish vote on Sunday.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in ⁠a snap general election on Sunday, despite adverse public polling suggesting a right-wing advantage.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” the Socialist leader told radio station SER on Friday, as political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning before the vote.
The outcome of the election will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys within five days of an election, Sanchez ⁠insisted that internal data suggested his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.
He said that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching ‌a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Earlier, during a televised pre-election debate, Sanchez clashed with PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Vox’s Santiago Abascal, as well as Ada Colau, a left-wing Spanish politician and former mayor of Barcelona associated with the Sumar political alliance, in a debate focused on immigration, the housing crisis and foreign policy.
The prime minister criticised the Madrid regional government, controlled by the PP, for awarding an honorary medal to the Israeli government while the assault on Gaza continued.
“It is shameful,” Sanchez said, accusing his opponents of having “no humanity whatsoever.”
He also interrupted Feijoo when the conservative leader described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “massacre”, insisting that “it is genocide”.
Sanchez warned voters that Spain faced a choice between “regression and progressivism”, arguing that the PP and Vox wanted to replicate the politics of US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with Trump and criticism of Israel. The dynamism of the EU’s fourth-largest economy under his leadership has also drawn praise at a turbulent time for global markets.
Sanchez is holding his final large rally in Madrid on Friday, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the “regression” of a possible PP-Vox coalition.
“We are unstoppable and we will win!” he told a Socialist meeting in the western city of Plasencia, sporting a red T-shirt emblazoned with the slogan “the power of women”.
He contrasted a Spain “of prosperity, principles and values” against a “reactionary coalition” that would question women’s rights, cut pensions and gut public services.
PP leader Feijoo, who won the most seats at the last election in 2023 but failed to form a government, told supporters in Barcelona: “This time we will pull it off.”
Dismissing Sanchez’s campaign of “fear”, he will hold his campaign finale in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region.
Addressing reporters before a closing rally in the eastern city of Valencia, Vox leader Abascal accused Sanchez’s “mafia-style” government of “betraying, robbing and lying” to the country.
Spaniards will observe a “day of reflection” on the ‌eve ‌of the vote on Saturday. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances
Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.
The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.
The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.
The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.
Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers .
In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.
“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”
He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.
However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.
In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.
It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”
The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.
Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.
Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.
However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.
“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.
Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.
He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.
The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.
A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.
In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.
International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.
On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.
The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.
“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.
He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.
After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.
Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.
He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
Pete Edochie starred in Netflix's first original Nigerian film, Lionheart
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.
"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.
"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.
Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.
If replicated across the state, that swing would translate into 67 seats for the Coalition – comfortably above the 45 needed to form a majority government. The Liberals and Nationals currently hold a combined 29 seats.
But the scale of Labor’s defeat remains unclear. Some polls have suggested the party could fall behind One Nation into third place, with its primary vote only marginally ahead of the Greens.
“Right now, definitely, it’s going to be a Coalition government, but how Labor, the Greens and One Nation are going to go – that’s going to be a lot more chaotic,” said Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room.
Raue said One Nation’s prospects will depend heavily on which party it is competing against in each seat. One Nation is targeting 12 lower house seats. It will field candidates in all lower house seats.
In contests with the Liberals or Nationals, One Nation would fare “very badly” because about 80% of preferences from other parties would flow to the Coalition partners, he said.
“The places where they are likely going to be strongest are those outer suburban seats they could take off Labor,” Raue said.
“They probably couldn’t take them if Labor was in a stronger position. Labor is so weak right now that those areas can come into play.”
On Friday, Labor campaign sources said they were bracing for a “wild night”, with three- and four-cornered contests expected across the state. Internal research suggested the party could lose up to 10 seats to One Nation, prompting former premier Steve Bracks to urge voters not to abandon Labor .
One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, tempered expectations, telling reporters on Friday: “We have effectively got one state member, anything more than that is a success. We have already won.”
Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a pollster with Redbridge, said Labor was at risk of losing more than 30 seats – a figure he described as conservative. The party currently holds 54.
“If they come out of this with 20 seats, it’s a really good result,” Samaras said. “Below that, without stating the obvious, it’s a massive problem.”
Samaras said Labor was likely to lose several regional seats, including Ripon, Bendigo East – held by former premier Jacinta Allan – Bendigo West, Eureka and Wendouree. The party could also lose seats across the Geelong region that it has held since 1999, including Bellarine, Geelong, Lara and South Barwon.
In Melbourne’s south-east, Carrum and Frankston were also at risk of switching from Labor to One Nation. Further out, Labor was not in contention in Bass, Hastings and Pakenham, where the contest was shaping as a fight between the Liberals and One Nation, he said.
In the north-west, Melton, Sunbury and Sydenham were also potential One Nation gains. Meanwhile, the Liberals are expected to pick up eastern suburbs seats including Ashwood, Bayswater, Box Hill, Glen Waverley and Ringwood.
The Liberals are even confident in the premier’s own seat of Niddrie and neighbouring Essendon.
Labor’s inner-city seats of Footscray, Northcote and Pascoe Vale were each a “coin toss” between the party and the Greens, Samaras said. But Greens sources are confident about the seats, as well as Prahran, which it lost to the Liberals at a 2025 byelection.
“The Coalition is going to win 55 to 60 seats but someone only has to breathe in the wrong direction and they lose 20,” he said.
The premier, Ben Carroll , made his final pitch to voters on Friday, saying while Labor had “made some mistakes”, it was the only party on the side of workers in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.
“We won’t fight against you. We won’t make cuts. We certainly won’t say one thing and then, after several million people have voted, then go and do another,” he said, in reference to the Coalition’s pre-budget costings on Thursday, which detailed a plan to privatise the sewage system.
The Coalition leader, Jess Wilson , called the poll a “a referendum on four more years of Labor”.
“Tomorrow Victorians have an opportunity to change the direction of the state we all love and we have the plan to get started,” she said.
If elected on Saturday, she will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

Europe wants to become more independent, competitive and secure. Yet it is precisely the tasks that are crucial to this that face the deepest cuts in the draft for the next EU budget. Behind this lies a structural problem in European politics.
The special Brussels summit on the European budget for the years 2028 to 2034 ended without agreement. On 17 December, the heads of state and government will meet again. Until then, the main question will be how much Europe is prepared to spend.
The European Commission has proposed a financial framework of just under €2 trillion. Council President António Costa has reduced this to around €1.78 trillion. Germany and other net contributors still consider that too high.
More revealing than the overall figure, however, is where Costa makes the cuts. Compared with the Commission’s draft, he removes around €95.5 billion from competitiveness, prosperity and security, and around €54 billion from agriculture, cohesion and related tasks. That amounts to reductions of 16 and 5% respectively. In defence industry, security and space, the cuts are almost 30%.
Costa’s draft does foresee substantial increases for defence and competitiveness compared with the current budget. Even so, the new strategic priorities are being cut disproportionately.
Germany and other net contributors want to limit their payments and focus the budget more strongly on competitiveness and security. Poland and other cohesion countries defend the funding for their regions. France wants an ambitious European budget while also protecting its agriculture. Italy takes a sceptical view of additional European levies.
Each of these positions is understandable from a national perspective. The problem arises from how they interact.
The European financial framework requires unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Every government can make its approval conditional on its own interests being safeguarded. This favours spending whose benefits can be clearly attributed to individual member states.
A French president can explain to farmers which subsidies he has secured in Brussels. A Polish prime minister can point to new roads and modernised regions. But which head of government can claim the benefit of a joint European air defence system purely for his or her own country?
Joint European tasks do have political advocates. But their benefits are less easily mapped onto the national balance sheet that underpins almost every budget negotiation in the end: how much did we pay in, and how much do we get back?
About 60% of the current European financial framework is devoted to agriculture and cohesion. Both areas serve core purposes of European integration: food security, economic development and the reduction of regional disparities.
However, Europe now has additional tasks to tackle that did not carry anything like the same weight when this budget structure was created.
Russia is threatening Europe’s security order. China has built up significant technological and industrial capacity in strategic sectors. The United States is pursuing its own economic and security interests, which do not necessarily coincide with Europes.
The conditions under which the bloc has built its prosperity in recent decades are changing fundamentally.
That cannot be addressed simply through higher national defence spending. It is equally about joint defence research, industrial production capacity, secure supply chains, cross-border energy networks, military mobility and European expertise in key technologies.
In 2024 Mario Draghi set out what would be needed: catching up the innovation gap with the United States and China, combining decarbonisation with competitiveness, and strengthening Europe’s security by reducing strategic dependencies. He put the additional private and public investment required at €750 to 800 billion a year.
This sum cannot and should not be financed solely from the European budget. However, the budget can mobilise national and private investment and make joint projects possible where individual member states cannot achieve the necessary scale on their own.
I believe the European budget should be shaped much more by its tasks. The decisive factor should be what the member states can achieve better, more efficiently or more cheaply together than alone.
Agriculture and the less developed regions of Europe still need reliability. But their shares of the budget should, with appropriate transition periods, gradually yet clearly decline in order to create more scope for joint investment in the future.
Anyone who thinks Europe can simply carry on as before is living off a substance that is steadily shrinking. A Europe that wants to become more sovereign and more independent also has to get ahead of events.
That calls for honesty on the revenue side. Costa’s draft sets aside €158 billion solely for repaying the EU debt taken on during the pandemic. This money is not available for other tasks.
Costa therefore proposes additional European sources of revenue, including levies on digital services provided by large companies, on tobacco and on non-recycled electronic waste. Anyone who rejects additional own resources has to explain whether they prefer higher national contributions or corresponding cuts. And anyone who demands more European tasks has to say how they should be funded.
The contribution rebates also belong in this context. They are the expression of a budget logic that measures the success of European policy by national returns. As long as this calculation dominates, funding joint tasks will remain structurally more difficult.
Germany and France are pushing for an understanding before the end of the year. Given the French presidential election next spring, that is understandable.
One possible compromise would be an even smaller overall volume combined with concessions to the net contributors, agriculture and the cohesion countries. Particularly contentious sources of revenue could be postponed, and funding for further aid to Ukraine could be negotiated separately.
Such an agreement would carry weight. It would create planning certainty and show that 27 governments, despite differing interests, are capable of reaching a compromise.
The crucial question, however, would be the price at which it is achieved. If the main effect is to protect established spending while once again making the new strategic tasks bear most of the savings, the underlying problem would remain.
Europe would still have to tackle many of its new tasks largely through national budgets, loans and additional financing instruments. Especially for long term investment in security, infrastructure and technological competitiveness, a lack of joint planning can lead to higher costs and avoidable duplication.
We do not have to turn all our challenges into European ones. But we should organise and fund at European level those we can no longer adequately handle at national level.
Anyone who wants a more sovereign and more independent Europe must also be prepared to draw fiscal policy conclusions from that.

6 Şubat 2023 depremlerinde ağır hasar gören Hatay’daki tarihî ve kültürel mirasın yeniden ayağa kaldırılmasına yönelik çalışmalar sürüyor. Kültür ve Turizm Bakanı Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Kırıkhan ilçesindeki Beyazıd-i Bestami Türbesi’nde düzenlenen törenle altı ilçede restorasyonu tamamlanan 20 vakıf eserini yeniden hizmete açtı.
Açılış töreninde konuşan Ersoy, depremlerin ardından Hatay’da 133 vakıf eserinin hasar gördüğünü, bunlardan 91’inin restorasyonunun tamamlandığını bildirdi. Kalan 42 eserin bir bölümünün yıl sonuna kadar, diğerlerinin ise Mayıs 2027’ye kadar tamamlanmasının hedeflendiğini söyledi.
Restorasyonu tamamlanan eserler arasında camiler, mescitler, türbeler, bir kilise, tarihî dükkânlar ve konuk evleri bulunuyor. Kırıkhan, Reyhanlı, Erzin, Antakya, Samandağ ve İskenderun’da yürütülen çalışmalar kapsamında 7 cami, 5 mescit ve 3 türbenin yanı sıra İskenderun Rum Katolik Kilisesi de yeniden ibadete açıldı.
Açılışı yapılan eserler arasında Kırıkhan’daki Beyazıd-i Bestami Türbesi, Antakya’daki Şeyh Abdurrahman Türbesi ile Şeyh İsa ve Şeyh Ali Bağdadi türbeleri yer aldı. Antakya’da Ali Çavuş, Debruz, Kerhan, Uçtum ve Züveroğlu mescitlerinin restorasyonları da tamamlandı.
Camilerdeki çalışmalar kapsamında depremde yıkılan minareler yeniden inşa edilirken hasar gören duvarlar, çatılar ve taşıyıcı sistemler onarıldı. Antakya’daki Semerciler Camii’nin yeniden inşasında yapının mevcut sütun ve sütun başlıkları korunarak özgün yerlerine yerleştirildi.
Hatay’ın çok kültürlü mirasının önemli yapılarından İskenderun Rum Katolik Kilisesi’nde ise Haziran 2023’te başlayan restorasyon çalışmaları tamamlandı. Bilim heyetinin gözetiminde ve koruma kurulunca onaylanan projeler doğrultusunda yürütülen çalışmalarda kilisenin taş ve tuğla duvarları onarıldı, taşıyıcı sistemi güçlendirildi; kapı, pencere ve çatıları restore edildi.
Restorasyon çalışmaları ibadethaneler ve türbelerle sınırlı kalmadı. Antakya’da Semerciler Camii ve Yeni Cami çevresindeki tarihî dükkânlar da yeniden inşa edildi. Yeni Cami çevresindeki 13 dükkânın aslına uygun biçimde yenilendiğini belirten Ersoy, Semerciler Camii çevresindeki dükkânların da restorasyonunun tamamlandığını söyledi.
Antakya’nın Kurtuluş Caddesi’nde bulunan ve 19’uncu yüzyılın başlarından günümüze ulaşan tarihî sivil mimari örneği yapı ile Samandağ’daki Vakıflı Köyü Konuk Evi de yeniden kullanıma kazandırıldı. Çalışmalarda yapıların özgün mimari özelliklerinin korunmasına özen gösterildi.
Ersoy, tarihî çarşıların ve dükkânların yeniden faaliyete geçmesinin kentin gündelik yaşamının toparlanması açısından önem taşıdığını belirterek esnafın yeniden kepenk açabilmesinin restorasyon çalışmalarının temel hedeflerinden biri olduğunu ifade etti.
Bakan Ersoy, deprem sonrasında Hatay’daki vakıf eserlerinin restorasyonu için bugüne kadar 4 milyar 308 milyon lira harcandığını açıkladı. Devam eden çalışmaların tamamlanmasıyla kent genelindeki toplam yatırımın yaklaşık 9 milyar 420 milyon liraya ulaşmasının öngörüldüğünü bildirdi.
Restorasyonların yalnızca yapıların fiziksel olarak onarılmasını değil, Hatay’ın kültürel hafızasının ve toplumsal yaşamının yeniden canlandırılmasını da amaçladığını belirten Ersoy, tamamlanan eserlerin ibadet, ziyaret ve ticaret hayatına yeniden katılmasının önemine dikkat çekti.

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.
However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.
Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.
Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs , turbans and yarmulkes.
Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."
Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.
"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.
CAQ ruled Quebec in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ) , which also supported Bill 21, formed government.
The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.
Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.
Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights .
"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.
He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.
Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to " Islamophobia as a state policy."

Liberals’ sewage plan ‘incredibly deceptive and dishonest, Greens leader says
Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Liberals had been “incredibly deceptive and dishonest” in not revealing the plans to lease Melbourne’s sewage plants until two days before the election after nearly half of Victorians had already voted.
double quotation mark There’s a reason that they hid this plan until nearly half of Victorians had already voted, because they know it’s a terrible plan that people would not support.
And if they were honest with the Victorian people earlier about their plans to sell off all our assets from under our feet, including our sewerage, I do not think that the Victorian community would support it.
And so I think if Jess Wilson does end up having a victory tonight, it won’t be an endorsement of her policies.
It’ll be a rejection of Labor and a rejection of the two party system that just isn’t working for people.
The Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell , told ABC’s Weekend Breakfast the Greens are competitive in seats Labor has held for 99 years, showing the “Greens surge is coming” amid disaffection with Labor.
double quotation mark What people are telling me is that they are just so dismayed and disappointed at how Labor has moved away from their traditional values.
They have really followed the Liberals and One Nation down a rightwing rabbit-hole, and people are sick of that.
They don’t want politicians that just keep taking donations from big corporations and then giving handouts to the gas industry or giving in to the gambling industry, or rolling out the red carpet for datacentres like Labor has done.
And that’s why they’re telling me that they’re voting Greens because they actually want a progressive voice that’s going to stand up for the values that this community cares about.
My colleague Benita Kolovos has informed me that the premier, Ben Carroll , voted at his old primary school St Christophers in Airport West, while the Liberal leader, Jess Wilson , voted at Our Lady of Good Counsel primary school in Deepdene.
Wilson told a reporter at the polling booth she was “confident of the victories statewide today” and downplayed what it would mean for her to become the first elected female premier in Victoria .
double quotation mark It’s not about me. If I’m given that honour, we’re absolutely ready and I’m ready. But this is about Victorians and fixing this state.
Carroll told reporters he was “fighting every day” for the state. He said:
double quotation mark I am confident because I’m getting that message. I’ve got it all day yesterday. People do feel like they’ve been sold down the river by the Liberal party, after 50% of Victorians voted, to come out with a radical privatisation agenda around kinder, renewables and water. People do feel very angry about that.
Going into the election, the Labor government is led by the premier, Ben Carroll . Carroll, who has only led Labor since late July, became leader after a spill against Jacinta Allan. Allan herself only became leader after the resignation of Daniel Andrews, who led Labor to the “Dan-slide” of 2018.
Victorian Labor has never won an election after changing leaders and this time they have done it twice. But Carroll has made an effort to distance himself from his predecessors saying, “I will do things differently”.
Jess Wilson is the Liberal leader, hoping to become the next premier. She became leader after a period of instability in the Victorian Liberal party that saw three leaders since the last election.
If she wins, she will be the youngest person to lead Victoria and the first woman to be elected premier. (Both Joan Kirner and Jacinta Allan became premier after their leaders resigned).
The Victorian Greens are led by Ellen Sandell . In 2014, she became the first Greens MP to be elected to Victoria’s lower house after campaigning against local toll roads.
Sandell hopes to take a page from progressive leaders around the world such as the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani . At the News24 leaders’ debate, Sandell outperformed Ben Carroll, according to an audience poll.
Leading the insurgent One Nation is Warren Pickering . He is running in the marginal Labor seat of Pakenham in Melbourne’s outer east. The former Australian army combat engineer was also a unsuccessful One Nation Senate candidate.
At the News24 leaders’ debate, Pickering was outperformed by Sandell but audiences still preferred him over Carroll.
The Coalition is poised to win 55 of 88 lower-house seats according to a YouGov poll of more than 4300 voters, commissioned by the Herald Sun and News24 and published on election eve.
One Nation would gain 12 seats and the Greens would add five more MPs to their pack of three, according to the analysis conducted between 6 and 23 November.
A Newspoll reported by The Australian late on Thursday had the Coalition extending to a 15-point lead over Labor on a two-party preferred basis.
The Coalition’s lead of 57.5% to Labor’s 42.5% compares with the Coalition’s 55-45 lead in October before the election campaign began.
If the polls are correct the Victorian Greens will have their most successful campaign on record, gaining between 13% and 17% of primary votes.
The party leader, Ellen Sandell , received the second-highest approval rating among undecided voters during the campaign’s only four-way leaders debate on 17 November.
Good morning, and welcome to the Victorian election live blog. I’m Josh Taylor and I will be taking you through until later this afternoon. Going into today, polls suggest the Coalition will comfortably win majority government, while Labor faces an electoral wipeout after 12 years in government, with suggestions the premier, Ben Carroll , could lose his own seat.
More than 2.2 million people had already voted as of Friday, according to the Victorian Electoral Commission, meaning nearly half of those eligible have already cast their vote.
Just as well, too, given the weather in Victoria today. Those democracy sausage sandwiches will be a little wet today with all the rain. There is a flood warning for parts of west, central and north-east Victoria, with possible minor flooding from Saturday morning for rivers including the Yarra. Rain is likely to continue throughout the day, easing into the evening with up to 30mm of rain expected in Melbourne. Now let’s get into it.

MasterChef 'in 26 Kasım akşamı yayınlanan yeni bölümünde Muhammed'in kaptan olduğu mavi takım ile Eyyüp Can'ın kaptan olduğu kırmızı takım bir kez daha karşı karşıya geldi. Haftanın ikinci dokunulmazlık oyununda takımlar, 7 çeşit Fransız yemeği hazırladı.
Hazırlık sürecinde mavi takımda Nice Salatası'nı hazırlayan Ayşe'ye sos konusunda Tolğa yardımcı oldu. Ancak hazırlanan sosu yoğun ve tat olarak keskin bulan Ayşe zeytinyağı ile açarak müdahale etti.
Tadım sırasında da Ayşe'nin sosu Tolğa ve Nilay'ın hazırladığını söylemesi üzerine Tolğa olanları şeflere anlattı. Şefler de kazanan tarafın kırmızı takım olduğunu, mavi takımın sosunun kıvamını çok akışkan bulduklarını, sebzelere bile yapışmadığını söyledi.
Tadım sonrası oyunu kazanan taraf kırmızı takım oldu. Şefler, bireysel dokunulmazlık için stüdyoya gelen mavi takımla salatayı konuştu.
Söz alan Ayşe, "Bu salata sosu meselesi daha sonuç açıklanmadan olay oldu. Tolğa beni kötülemeye başladı tuhaf bir şekilde" deyince Tolğa araya girdi.
Sinirlenen Tolğa, "Bunlarla tartışmak kadar kötü bir şey yok. Kendisine olması gerekeni söyledim ama kabul etmedi. Reçete kendisinin de ben de geri çekildim. Seni kötüleyecek bir tane cümlemi söyleyin ben buradan diskalifiye olmak istiyorum. Yeter. Ben bunlarla mı uğraşacağım şefim?" dedi.
Sonrasında sözünü bitiren Ayşe, sosun daha sıvı olması gerektiğini düşündüğünü tadını da beğenmeyince müdahale ettiğini belirtti ve "Daha yemeğin sonucu açıklanmadan ‘ben sosu çok güzel yaptım da senin yüzünden böyle oldu’ demek takım arkadaşına saygısızlık" dedi.
Bunun üzerine Tolğa, "Bence burada bir kadınla konuşmak tamamen saygısızlık. Merhaba demek bile MasterChef'te saygısızlık. Bence bunlar böyle. Kime bir şeyler söylersek bu onu algılıyor" deyince Somer Şef araya girdi.
Somer Sivrioğlu, "Yine de genelleme yapmayalım. Kadın olarak deme. Ayşe'yle öyle olabilir" dedi.
Tolğa da "Şefim ben burada hangi kadına bir şey söylesem ben saygısızmışım, kötülemişim. Öyle bir şey olmamasına rağmen oldu diyorlar. Ben bunlardan gerçekten bıktım, ben bunlarla uğraşmak istemiyorum şefim" dedi.
Somer Şef bunun üzerine "Tolğacığım konu Ayşe ya Ayşe hakkında yap. Kadınlar hakkında diye niye bir genelleme yapıyorsun?" dedi.
Tolğa'nın Somer Şef'e "Siz de önünü kesiyorsunuz" itirazıyla Somer Şef sinirlendi.
"Tolğacığım ben senin jürinim. İster sözünü keserim, ister dışarı atarım saygısızlık yapma. Sana bir laf söylüyorum. Ben burada seni korumaya çalışıyorum. Sana yardımcı olmak mı suç? Ne konuşursan konuş" diyerek stüdyoyu terk etti.
Somer Şef gittikten sonra Mehmet Şef hak verince Tolğa da "Hiç de haklı değil. Ben hepsinden aynı tepkiyi görüyorum şefim" dedi.
Bunun ardından Mehmet Yalçınkaya da "Diğer arkadaşlarınla da sorun yaşasan onlara bunları o gün söylersin. Bunu genelleme yapamayız, erkekler için de yapamayız. Ama Somer Şef dediğinde haklı ve gerçekten seni korumaya çalışıyor" ifadelerini kullandı.
Tüm bunların ardından mavi takım, bireysel dokunulmazlık için tekrar tezgah başına geçti. Yarışmacılar, “Prik Nam Pla ve Çıtırlı Kai Jeow” adlı yemeği hazırladı.
En iyi tabağı hazırlayarak bireysel dokunulmazlığı kazanan isim Muhammed oldu. Takım oylaması sonrası da eleme adayı Ayşe oldu.

An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.
EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.
Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.
There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.
"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.
The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.
Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."
Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.
Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.
In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).
"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."
Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.
"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.
Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.
Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.
They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.
In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.
The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.
The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.
But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.
"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.
There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.
The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen , the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.
EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."
Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.
"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."
EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.
